title: Infant communion once treated as apostolic — later abrogated by Rome herself
source_text: XXXVIII. Imo olim inter Christianos, praesertim in Ecclesia Romana atque Africana, & quidem per multa saecula, obtinuit consuetudo infantibus praebendi sacram Eucharistiam statim atque baptizati essent: istudque ad eorum salutem necessarium existimabatur, ut patet ex Cypriano lib. de lapsis num. 20. ex Innocentio primo Episcopo Romano in epist. ad Concil. Milevit. Item ex Gelasio Episcopo quoque Romano, in epist. ad omnes Episcopos per Picenum, & ex Augustino pluribus in locis. Qui sententiam istam de necessitate sacrae Eucharistiae respectu infantium non simpliciter probant, sed illam proferunt tanquam totius Ecclesiae sui temporis communem, adeoque ex Apostolica traditione descendentem, & inde tanquam ex re nota atque concessa argumenta ducunt adversus Pelagianos, ut speciatim videre est apud Augustinum libro 1. de peccati meritis & remissione cap. 24. & lib. 1. contra Julianum cap. 2. Nec est ullus scriptorum istius aevi qui reclamet. Idque agnoscunt ipsi Doctores Pontificii, ut Vasquez tom. 3. in 3. Thom. disp. 212. cap. 2. & Maldonat. in Joan. 6. num. 116. ubi dicit sententiam illam Augustini & Innocentii sexcentos circiter annos in Ecclesia viguisse. Et tamen haec consuetudo in Ecclesia Romana pridem abrogata est, sic a concilio Tridentino damnata. Si igitur jam olim primis post Christum temporibus traditiones non scriptae tam incertae & variae erant inter ipsos fideles & Doctores Ecclesiae, qui saepe traditionum obtentu decepti sunt, quid jam amplius certi post saecula sexdecim ex traditionibus haberi posse existimabimus? Et quam intutum atque periculosum erit illas assumere pro fidei regula, & ipsis Scripturis sacris authoritate aequare.
pass_a_gloss: Indeed formerly among Christians, especially in the Roman and African Church, and that through many ages, the custom obtained of giving the sacred Eucharist to infants as soon as they were baptized: and that was thought necessary to their salvation, as is plain from Cyprian, On the Lapsed, number 20; from Innocent I, bishop of Rome, in his letter to the Council of Milevis; likewise from Gelasius, also bishop of Rome, in his letter to all the bishops through Picenum; and from Augustine in many places. Who do not simply approve that opinion about the necessity of the sacred Eucharist with respect to infants, but bring it forward as the common opinion of the whole Church of their time, and so descending from Apostolic tradition, and from it as from a known and conceded matter they draw arguments against the Pelagians, as may be seen especially in Augustine, book 1 On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins, chapter 24, and book 1 Against Julian, chapter 2. Nor is there any writer of that age who protests. And the Pontifical doctors themselves acknowledge this, as Vasquez volume 3 on the third part of Thomas, disputation 212, chapter 2, and Maldonatus on John 6, number 116, where he says that opinion of Augustine and Innocent flourished in the Church about six hundred years. And yet this custom was long ago abrogated in the Roman Church, and so condemned by the Council of Trent. If therefore already of old in the first times after Christ unwritten traditions were so uncertain and various among the faithful themselves and the doctors of the Church, who were often deceived by the pretext of traditions, what more of certainty shall we think can be had from traditions after sixteen centuries? And how unsafe and dangerous will it be to take them up as a rule of faith and to equal them in authority with the sacred Scriptures themselves?
pass_b_english: Still stronger: for many ages, especially in the Roman and African churches, infants received the Eucharist as soon as they were baptized, and it was held necessary to their salvation.

Witnesses: Cyprian On the Lapsed; Innocent I to Milevis; Gelasius to the Picene bishops; Augustine in many places — not as a private whim but as the common Church view descending from apostolic tradition, and used as conceded ground against the Pelagians.
No contemporary writer objects. Roman doctors admit it: Vasquez and Maldonatus note Augustine's and Innocent's view held about six hundred years.
Yet Rome long ago abolished the custom, and Trent condemned it.
If unwritten traditions were already so uncertain and various in the first Christian centuries — and often deceived even good doctors — what certainty can sixteen later centuries add?
How unsafe, then, to take them as a rule of faith and set them equal in authority with sacred Scripture.
